title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
My first weeks in the UBC Master of Data Science program have been an amazing experience. Returning to school after spending time in the workforce has reawakened my love of learning. However, adjusting to the program’s fast-paced schedule has certainly been challenging.
One thing that surprised me was the diversity of ages and professional experiences within the cohort. So far, I have been learning how to use tools and technologies such as Git, NumPy, R, and Quarto for data-science projects.
Although the program has been challenging, I am excited to continue developing my programming and analytical skills. I am especially looking forward to learning how to apply data science to make data-driven marketing decisions.

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text: How did the percentage of Canadians reporting fruit and vegetable consumption five or more times per day change between 2015 and 2021?

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text: How did the percentage of Canadians reporting fruit and vegetable consumption five or more times per day change between 2015 and 2021?

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text:
Data source
The data come from Statistics Canada’s Canadian Indicator Framework, indicator 3.1.1.
This indicator measures how frequently people report eating fruits and vegetables, not the number of servings or the amount consumed.
The data are available under the Statistics Canada Open Licence.
Adapted from Statistics Canada, Canadian Indicator Framework, indicator 3.1.1, reference years 2015–2021. This does not constitute an endorsement by Statistics Canada of this product.

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text:
Prepare the data
I keep the available observations from 2015 through 2021 to match my research question. I select the year and percentage, give the percentage column a clearer name, and sort the observations by year.

selected_years = (nutrition_raw["Year"] >= 2015) & (nutrition_raw["Year"] <= 2021)

nutrition = nutrition_raw.loc[selected_years, ["Year", "Value"]].copy()

nutrition = nutrition.rename(columns={"Value": "Percentage"})

nutrition = nutrition.sort_values("Year")

The prepared data contain five observations. The downloaded dataset has no observations for 2018 or 2019, so I leave those years missing rather than treating them as zero. The empty GeoCode column is not needed for this analysis.

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text:
Calculate the change
I compare the first and last percentages in the prepared data. Subtracting the 2015 percentage from the 2021 percentage gives the change in percentage points.

first_percentage = nutrition["Percentage"].iloc[0]
last_percentage = nutrition["Percentage"].iloc[-1]

change_pp = last_percentage - first_percentage

print(f"2015: {first_percentage:.1f}%")
print(f"2021: {last_percentage:.1f}%")
print(f"Change: {change_pp:.1f} percentage points")

2015: 31.5%
2021: 21.8%
Change: -9.7 percentage points


The reported percentage decreased from 31.5% in 2015 to 21.8% in 2021. This is a decrease of 9.7 percentage points, not a 9.7% relative decrease.
This calculation describes the difference between the published estimates. It does not explain why the estimates changed. ## Visualize the trend
I plot the percentage for each available year. Each dot represents a published observation. The connecting lines help show the pattern, but they do not provide estimates for the missing years.

plt.figure(figsize=(7, 4))

plt.plot(
    nutrition["Year"],
    nutrition["Percentage"],
    marker="o"
)

plt.title("Fruit and vegetable consumption in Canada")
plt.xlabel("Year")
plt.ylabel("Reported percentage (%)")

plt.xticks(range(2015, 2022))
plt.ylim(0, 40)

plt.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()







Figure 1: Percentage reporting fruit and vegetable consumption five or more times per day, Canada (excluding territories), available years from 2015 to 2021. Source: Statistics Canada.

title: Fruit and Vegetable Consumption in Canada
text:
Conclusion
The published percentage reporting fruit and vegetable consumption five or more times per day decreased from 31.5% in 2015 to 21.8% in 2021, a decline of 9.7 percentage points.
The percentage was lower at each successive observation in this dataset. However, observations are missing for 2018 and 2019, so the data do not show what happened in every individual year.
This is a descriptive comparison of published estimates, not a test of statistical significance. The indicator measures reported eating frequency rather than portion sizes or overall diet quality, and this analysis does not establish why the estimates changed.
